verb:raven.tx: From Rave + -en, possibly after English (to) rave.

verb:regnen.tx: From Middle High German regenen, from Old High German reganōn, derived from the noun at hand in modern Regen (“rain”). Cognate with Hunsrik rehne and Yiddish רעגענען (regenen).

noun:Rom.tx: From Middle High German Rōme, from Old High German Rōma, a relatinisation of Rūma, from Proto-West Germanic *Rūmu.

verb:rotten.tx: From Middle Low German rotten, alteration (perhaps intensivation) of older rōten, from Old Saxon rotōn, from Proto-West Germanic *rotēn.

adj:rein.tx: From Middle High German reine, from Old High German reini, from Proto-West Germanic *hrainī, from Proto-Germanic *hrainiz, from Proto-Indo-European *króy-n-is, from *krey- (“divide, sift”). Cognate with Old Saxon hreni, (Low German ren), Dutch rein, Old Norse hreinn (Swedish ren), Ancient Greek κρῑ́νω (krī́nō, “separate, decide, judge”), Old Irish criathar, English riddle (“sieve”).

adv:rein.tx: From Middle High German reine, from Old High German reini, from Proto-West Germanic *hrainī, from Proto-Germanic *hrainiz, from Proto-Indo-European *króy-n-is, from *krey- (“divide, sift”). Cognate with Old Saxon hreni, (Low German ren), Dutch rein, Old Norse hreinn (Swedish ren), Ancient Greek κρῑ́νω (krī́nō, “separate, decide, judge”), Old Irish criathar, English riddle (“sieve”).

adj:rot.tx: From Middle High German rōt (“red, red-haired”), from Old High German rōt (“red, scarlet, purple-red, brown-red, yellow-red”), from Proto-West Germanic *raud, from Proto-Germanic *raudaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rowdʰós, from *h₁rewdʰ-. Compare Low German root, rod, rot, Dutch rood, English red, West Frisian read, Danish rød.

adj:real.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin reālis. Doublet of reell.

noun:Rappen.tx: From a variant of Alemannic German Rapp (“raven”). Doublet of Rabe.

verb:rauben.tx: From Middle High German rouben, from Old High German roubōn, from Proto-West Germanic *raubōn, from Proto-Germanic *raubōną.

noun:Räuber.tx: From Middle High German röubære, roubære, roubāre, from Old High German roubāri, equivalent to rauben + -er or Raub + -er.

noun:Raum.tx: From Middle High German rūm, from Old High German rūm, from Proto-West Germanic *rūm, from Proto-Germanic *rūmą, from Proto-Indo-European *rewh₁-.

noun:Rebe.tx: From Middle High German rëbe, from Old High German rëba, from Proto-West Germanic *rebā.

adj:recht.tx: From Middle High German rëht, from Old High German rëht, from Proto-West Germanic *reht (“right, straight”). Cognates Cognate with Yiddish רעכט (rekht), Icelandic réttur, Dutch recht, English right, Danish ret.

adv:recht.tx: From Middle High German rëht, from Old High German rëht, from Proto-West Germanic *reht (“right, straight”). Cognates Cognate with Yiddish רעכט (rekht), Icelandic réttur, Dutch recht, English right, Danish ret.

verb:rennen.tx: From a merger of transitive / causative Old High German rennan (“to make something run or flow”) (from Proto-Germanic *rannijaną), and intransitive Old High German rinnan (“to run or flow”) (from Proto-Germanic *rinnaną). A similar development of merging roots can be seen in Dutch rennen and English run as well.

noun:RNA.tx: Borrowed from English RNA, from ribonucleic acid.

noun:Reifen.tx: Stem variant of Reif, which developed weak forms in early modern German.

adj:royal.tx: From French royal, from Latin regalis. Occasionally attested in the 19th century and perhaps earlier. More regular use dates from the latter half of the 20th century, reinforced by English royal; compare die Royals (“the British royal family”). The derivatives Royalist, Royalismus are older in German.

verb:regen.tx: From Middle High German regen (“to make protrude, to erect, to excite, to move”), from Proto-West Germanic *hraggjan (“to make stand, wake up, incite”). By synchronic analysis, the causative of ragen.

adj:rank.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German rank, ranc, from Old Saxon *rank, from Proto-West Germanic *rank.

adj:renal.tx: Learned borrowing from Late Latin renalis, from Latin rēnēs (“kidneys”).

verb:reden.tx: From Middle High German reden, from Old High German redōn, rediōn (“to speak”), a derivative of reda, redia (“speech, word, opinion, view, mind”), from Proto-Germanic *raþjǭ, *raþjō (“accountability, speech”). See Rede.

noun:Rinde.tx: From Middle High German rinde, rinte, from Old High German rinda, rinta, from Proto-West Germanic *rindā, from Proto-Germanic *rindǭ.

adj:reich.tx: From Middle High German rīche, from Old High German rīhhi (“rich, mighty”), from Proto-West Germanic *rīkī, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz, a derivative of *rīks (“king, ruler”), itself a borrowing from Proto-Celtic *rīxs (compare Irish rí). All from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to rule”), from which Latin rēx is derived. See also German Reich. Cognates include Danish rig, Dutch rijk, English …

noun:Rabbi.tx: From Latin rabbi. Doublet of Rabbiner and Rebbe.

noun:Rad.tx: From Middle High German rat, from Old High German rad, from Proto-West Germanic *raþ, from Proto-Germanic *raþą, from Proto-Indo-European *Hret- (“to roll”). Related to Swedish ratt (“steering wheel”) and Finnish ratti (“steering wheel”). Also related to English rotary and Spanish rueda (“wheel”), which descended from the same PIE root through Latin rota.

noun:Radio.tx: Circa 1920, from English radio, short for radiotelegraphy.

noun:Rain.tx: From Middle High German rein, which also appears in reinkurni, reinifano (“tansy”), Modern German Rainfarn, for this plant’s growing as field mark, from Old High German rein (“wall, baulk, ridge”), from Proto-West Germanic *rain, from Proto-Germanic *rainō. Cognate with Icelandic rein, Swedish ren, English rean (“ridge, furrow, gutter”), French rain, Lithuanian rai̇̃vė (“furrow”), Latvian riêva …

noun:Rand.tx: From Middle High German rant, from Old High German rant, from Proto-Germanic *randō, which according to Duden is related to *hramō (“framework”). Pokorny prefers a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rem- (“to rest”). Cognate with English rand.

noun:Rang.tx: 17th century, borrowed from French rang. Doublet of Ring.

noun:Range.tx: From an East Central German word for “sow on heat”, derived from Middle High German rangen (“to run back and forth”), from the root of Proto-Germanic *wringaną (“to wring”). Related with wringen and rangeln (“to scrap, wrestle”). Note that the loss of initial w- in Range is simply the regular High German development, whereas in rangeln (which is of Low German origin) it has a different reason; see the lemma.

noun:Rapport.tx: 17th century, borrowed from French rapport. The use in psychology probably after English rapport.

noun:Rat.tx: From Middle High German rāt, from Old High German rāt, from Proto-West Germanic *rād, from Proto-Germanic *rēdaz. Cognate with Dutch raad, English rede and read (noun).

noun:Rate.tx: Ca. 1500, from Latin rata, perhaps through Italian rata and/or Middle French rate.

noun:Ratio.tx: 16th century, from Latin ratio. Doublet of Räson, Ration, and Rede.

noun:Rauch.tx: From Middle High German rouch, from Old High German rouh, from Proto-West Germanic *rauki, from Proto-Germanic *raukiz. Compare Low German Röök, Dutch rook, English reek, Danish røg, Swedish rök. See also riechen, from a related root.

noun:Rebus.tx: Derived from Latin rebus. Cognate with English rebus, French rébus.

noun:Recht.tx: From Middle High German rëht, from Old High German rëht, from Proto-West Germanic *reht, from Proto-Germanic *rehtą (“right, privilege”). Compare Dutch recht, English right, Danish ret, Swedish rätt.

noun:Reck.tx: From Low German and Middle Low German recke (“crossbar”), ultimately from the root of Rah (“yard”). Cognate with Dutch rek (“pole, clothes-horse”).

noun:Referendum.tx: From Latin referendum. Much reinforced in recent years by English referendum.

noun:Regal.tx: Early 17th century, of unclear origin. Hypotheses include: * Derived from Proto-Germanic *rigǭ ~ *rīgǭ ~ *rīhǭ, whence German Riege and Reihe (both originally “row, line”). * Derived from Latin rēgula, whence German Riegel (“bar, latch”), Dutch richel (“bar, latch”, dialectally also “rack”). In both of the above cases the derivative must have been influenced by Latin or Romance. Earlier Low …

noun:Regen.tx: From Middle High German rëgen, from Old High German rëgan, from Proto-West Germanic *regn, from Proto-Germanic *regną. Cognate with Yiddish רעגן (regn), Dutch regen, English rain, Danish regn.

noun:Regenbogen.tx: From Middle High German rëgenboge, from Old High German reginbogo, from Proto-West Germanic *regnabogō. Equivalent to Regen (“rain”) + Bogen (“bow, arch, arc”). Compare Dutch regenboog, English rainbow, Yiddish רעגנבויגן (regnboygn), Danish regnbue, Icelandic regnbogi.

noun:Regime.tx: Borrowed from French régime, from Latin regimen.

noun:Reich.tx: From Middle High German rīche, from Old High German rīhhi (“power, might, empire”), from Proto-West Germanic *rīkī, from Proto-Germanic *rīkiją, itself either a substantivised *rīkijaz (“rich, mighty”) (whence also German reich (“rich”)), or a direct borrowing from a Celtic language; compare Old Irish ríge (“rule, kingship”). Cognates include Old English rīċe (“kingdom, empire”) (Middle English …

noun:Reis.tx: From Middle High German rīs, borrowed from Late Latin rīsum or rīsus, from Latin orȳza, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄρῡζα (órūza) (Greek όρυζα (óryza)). See also English rice.

noun:Relief.tx: 18th century, from French relief, itself semantically after Italian rilievo.

noun:Ren.tx: From Early Modern German reen, ultimately from Old Norse hreinn (compare Swedish ren, Danish ren, Norwegian Nynorsk rein), from Proto-Germanic *hrainaz, most likely from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“head, top; horn”) as in “horned animal”, thus distantly related to Hirsch, Hornisse, Rind as well as Hirn, Horn. The compound Rentier (corresponding to English reindeer) is more commonly used.

noun:Rentier.tx: 17th century, from Ren (“reindeer”) + Tier (“animal”), following Danish rensdyr, Swedish rendjur, from Old Norse hreindýri.

noun:Requiem.tx: Borrowed from Latin requiem (“rest”, accusative singular), from the beginning of the text that is spoken in the mass: Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine.

noun:Reserve.tx: Borrowed from French réserve, from Latin reservāre (“save back”), from re- (“back”) + servāre (“to save, to keep”).

noun:Resignation.tx: 15th century in the obsolete sense, from Middle French resignation, from Latin resignatio. The contemporary sense since the 18th century, from Modern French résignation.

noun:Rest.tx: Borrowed from Italian resto, from restare (“to remain”), from Latin restō.

noun:Reuse.tx: From Middle High German riuse, from Old High German rūsa, riusa (10th century), of uncertain origin; perhaps the s represents grammatischer Wechsel of r and the word is a jōn- stem from the root of Rohr (“reed”). Cognate with Swedish ryssja, Danish ruse, Norwegian Bokmål ruse.

noun:Rind.tx: From Middle High German rint, from Old High German rind, hrind, from Proto-West Germanic *hrinþ, from Proto-Germanic *hrinþaz. Cognate with Middle Dutch rint. Also related with modern Dutch rund (from Middle Dutch runt), English rother.

noun:Ring.tx: From Middle High German rinc, from Old High German ring, from Proto-West Germanic *hring, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz, cognate with Danish ring, Dutch ring, English ring, Swedish ring.

noun:Ritter.tx: From Middle High German ritter, from Middle Dutch ridder, Flemish byform of rîder, from rîden + -er (equivalent to German reiten + -er). In Middle High German, both ritter and rīter (whence modern Reiter) were used in the sense of “horseman”, “mounted man-at-arms”, as well as for the (emerging) rank of “knight”, and, by generalisation, any member of the lower nobility. Gradually, both forms were …

noun:Rock.tx: From Middle High German roc, from Old High German roc, from Proto-West Germanic *hrokk, from Proto-Germanic *hrukkaz, from Proto-Indo-European *rukn-, *ruk-, *rug-, *ruǵ- (“to spin”); or perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *kreḱ- (“to weave”). Doublet of Frack.

noun:Rose.tx: Inherited from Middle High German rôse, from Old High German rōsa, from Latin rosa.

noun:Rubidium.tx: Borrowed from New Latin rūbidium, derived by German chemist R. W. Bunsen in 1861, from Latin rūbidus (“red”) because its spectrum has two red lines.

noun:Rucksack.tx: From Alemannic German Ruggsack, equivalent to Standard German Rücken (“back”) + Sack (“sack”). Compare Dutch rugzak, English rucksack, Danish rygsæk, Russian рюкзак (rjukzak), and Swedish ryggsäck.

noun:Ruin.tx: Borrowed from French ruine, from Latin ruīna. Doublet of Ruine.

noun:Rune.tx: From Middle High German rūne, from Old High German rūna, from Proto-West Germanic *rūnu, from Proto-Germanic *rūnō.

noun:Rahmen.tx: From Middle High German ram, rame f (“column, frame”), from Old High German rama f (“support”), from Proto-West Germanic *hramu (“frame, support”). Cognate with Hunsrik Raume, Dutch raam n.

verb:röntgen.tx: From the noun Röntgen (“X-ray”), with -en reinterpreted as the infinitive ending of a verb.

noun:Rolltreppe.tx: Ca. 1898, from rollen (“to roll”) + Treppe (“staircase”), possibly after French escalier roulant (of roughly contemporaneous attestation).

verb:rollen.tx: From Middle High German rollen, from Old French roeler, from Medieval Latin rotulāre, from Latin rotula.

noun:Rasse.tx: From French race, from Italian razza.

adj:richtig.tx: From Middle High German rihtec, from Old High German rihtīg, from reht (“right”) + -ig. Equivalent to recht + -ig. Originally only an adjective; adverb developed later.

adv:richtig.tx: From Middle High German rihtec, from Old High German rihtīg, from reht (“right”) + -ig. Equivalent to recht + -ig. Originally only an adjective; adverb developed later.

verb:richten.tx: From Middle High German richten, from Old High German rihten, from Proto-West Germanic *rihtijan (“to right”). Cognate with English right.

noun:Richter.tx: From Middle High German rihtære, rihter, from Old High German rihtāri. By surface analysis, agent noun of richten. Cognates include Dutch rechter and Old English rihtere.

noun:Riese.tx: From Middle High German rise, from Old High German riso, risi, from Proto-West Germanic *risi (“giant”). Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål rise (“mountain troll”) and Dutch reus (“giant”).

noun:Rahm.tx: Dialectal variant of expected Raum (early modern German, rare), from Middle High German roum, from Old High German roum, from Proto-West Germanic *raum, from Proto-Germanic *raumaz. The form Rahm ousted the regular form due to homonymy with Raum (“room”), from Middle High German rūm. Dialects that have developed Middle High German -ou- into -ā- are found in south-eastern and central-western …

noun:Raub.tx: From Middle High German roup, from Old High German roub, from Proto-West Germanic *raub, from Proto-Germanic *raubaz. More at robe.

verb:reifen.tx: From Middle High German rīfen, from Old High German rīfen.

noun:Rausch.tx: From Middle High German rūsch, from Middle High German rūschen. More at rauschen. Compare Dutch roes, English rush.

adj:russisch.tx: From Middle High German rūzesch, from Rūz, from Old High German Rūzo, from Medieval Latin Russus, from Medieval Greek Ῥῶς (Rhôs). By surface analysis, Russe + -isch.

noun:Röhre.tx: From Middle High German rōre (“reed, rush”), rœre, from Old High German rōra, a derivative of rōr (whence Rohr, which see).

noun:Rohr.tx: From Middle High German rōr, from Old High German rōr, from Proto-West Germanic *rauʀ; compare English rush and Old Norse reyrr, also possibly related to Latin ruscum (“bark”). Cognate with Hunsrik Roher, Danish rør, Swedish rör.

verb:rauchen.tx: From Middle High German rouchen, röuchen, from Old High German rouhhen, from Proto-West Germanic *raukijan. By surface analysis, Rauch (“smoke”) + -en. The form without umlaut is due to (chiefly Upper German) umlaut hindrance before velars and/or readaptation to the noun. Some dialects use either form throughout, others came to distinguish both forms (transitive vs. intransitive). In the latter …

verb:räuchern.tx: 15th century, iterative extension of obsolete räuchen, from Middle High German röuchen, byform of rouchen, whence modern German rauchen (“to smoke”), which see for more. Both from Proto-Germanic *raukijaną. By surface analysis, Rauch + -ern. Compare Luxembourgish reecheren, Hunsrik reichre.

noun:Robbe.tx: Borrowed from Low German robbe, rubbe, in Middle Low German meaning “rabbit." Of uncertain ultimate origin; compare English rabbit, French rabot (“plane”). Or, possibly related to Latvian rups (“coarse, rough”), referring to the whiskers. Also compared is the personal name Robbe. Has also been compared to English rub, referring to seals' movements, but this is unlikely.

noun:Ratte.tx: From Middle High German ratte, from Old High German ratta, rato, from Proto-West Germanic *ratt, from Proto-Germanic *rattaz (“rat”); see that entry and English rat for more. Compare also Dutch rat, Swedish råtta, French rat. The consonantism ratta in Old High German (instead of *razza) is unexplained. One possible explanation is that the form was borrowed from Old Saxon ratta. The dialectal …

noun:Rüssel.tx: With irregular shortening of the stem vowel from Middle High German rüeȥel, from Old High German *ruoȥil, from Proto-West Germanic *wrōtil. Compare typologically Polish ryj, Russian ры́ло (rýlo) (akin to рыть (rytʹ)).

noun:Raupe.tx: From northern Middle High German rūpe, from Middle Low German rūpe, itself perhaps from Proto-Germanic *rūpō and then probably related with *raupijaną, whence German raufen (“to pluck, pick, harvest”). Cognate with Middle Dutch rupe, whence dialectal Dutch ruip. Also related with standard Dutch rups.

noun:Rücken.tx: From Middle High German rücke, from Old High German rucki, akin to Old Saxon hruggi, both from Proto-West Germanic *hrugi, from Proto-Germanic *hrugjaz. More at ridge.

noun:Rost.tx: From Middle High German rost, from Old High German rost, from Proto-West Germanic *rust, from Proto-Germanic *rustaz (“rust”), from Proto-Indo-European *rudʰso- (“red”), from *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”).

noun:Rogen.tx: From Middle High German rogen and roge, from Old High German rogan, rogin, *hrogan and rogo (“roe”), from Proto-Germanic *hrugnaz and *hrugô (“roe”). Of uncertain origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *krek- (“frogspawn”). Compare Low German Rögen, Dutch roge, English roe, Danish rogn. More at roe.

noun:Rapunzel.tx: Probably borrowed from 16th century Italian raponzolo, dialectal diminutive of Italian rapa (“turnip”), from Latin rāpa, from the neuter plural of rāpum.

noun:Rettich.tx: From Middle High German retich, from Old High German retich, rātih, from Proto-West Germanic *radik, *rādik. Doublet of Radix.

verb:reizen.tx: Middle High German reizen, Old High German reiʒen, Proto-Germanic *raitijaną

noun:Reise.tx: From Middle High German reise, reis, from Old High German reisa, from Proto-West Germanic *raisu.

adj:rar.tx: From Latin rārus, chiefly through French rare.

adj:reell.tx: Borrowed from French réel. Doublet of real.

adj:roh.tx: From Middle High German rō, from Old High German (h)rō, from Proto-West Germanic *hrau, from Proto-Germanic *hrawaz, from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂-. Cognate with Dutch rauw, English raw. In Old High German only the uninflected stem was monophthongised to -ō. Various ways of levelling yielded many variants in Middle High German (including rō, rōch, rou, rā). The contemporary form has been …

adj:reif.tx: From Middle High German rīfe, from Old High German rīfi, akin to Old Saxon rīpi (Modern Dutch rijp).

verb:reißen.tx: From Middle High German rīȥen, from Old High German rīȥan (“to scratch”), from a conflation of two similar verbs:. * Proto-West Germanic *wrītan, from Proto-Germanic *wrītaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline”) * Proto-West Germanic *hrītan, from Proto-Germanic *hrītaną. Cognate with English rat (“to rip up, tear, rend”), Dutch rijten (“to rip up, tear, …

verb:reiten.tx: From Middle High German rīten, from Old High German rītan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīdan, from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną. A Proto-Indo-European *reydʰ- preform does not exist, only northwest-European forms. Cognate with Dutch rijden, Low German rieden, English ride, Danish ride, Swedish rida.

noun:Rache.tx: From Middle High German rāche, from Old High German rāhha, from Proto-West Germanic *wrāku, from Proto-Germanic *wrēkō (“persecution, revenge”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“to drive”). Cognate with archaic English wreak (“revenge”). The irregular short vowel in modern German is due to the inherited short vowel in the verb rächen, reinforced by a spelling pronunciation among Low German …

noun:Rachen.tx: From Middle High German rache, from Old High German rahho, hrahho, from Proto-West Germanic *hrakō, from Proto-Germanic *hrakô, from Proto-Indo-European *kreg- (“to croak, crow”). Cognate with Old English hraca (“throat”). Related also to English retch (“to clear one's throat”), Icelandic hráki (“spit, saliva”).

noun:Ruf.tx: From Middle High German ruof, from Old High German hruof, ruof, from ruofan (“to call”). Compare Dutch roep, Low German Rop (dialectal Raup)).

verb:rufen.tx: From Middle High German ruofen, from Old High German ruofan, hruofan, from Proto-West Germanic *hrōpan, from Proto-Germanic *hrōpaną. Cognate with Dutch roepen, English roop, which see. Alongside there existed a weak Middle High German ruofen, from Old High German (h)ruofen. Weak conjugation is attestable until the 19th century. It indirectly lingers in the umlautless present forms, as against …

noun:Rotz.tx: From Middle High German rotz, roz, from Old High German roz, hroz, from Proto-West Germanic *hrott, *hrot, *hrutt (“snot, slime”), which is likely ultimately of imitative origin. Cognate with Old English hrot. Possibly related with Old High German hrūzan, Old English hrūtan (“to snore”). Compare also Ancient Greek κόρυζα (kóruza, “mucus”).

verb:riechen.tx: From Middle High German riechen, from Old High German riohhan, from Proto-West Germanic *reukan, from Proto-Germanic *reukaną. Compare English reek, Dutch rieken, Danish ryge, Swedish ryka. See also Rauch, Geruch.

noun:Rute.tx: From Middle High German ruote, from Old High German ruota, from Proto-Germanic *rōdō. Akin to Old Saxon rōda, compare Hunsrik Rut, Dutch roede and English rod and rood (“cross”).

verb:retten.tx: From Middle High German retten, from Old High German hretten or retten, from Proto-West Germanic *hraddjan, from Proto-Germanic *hradjaną (“to save, rescue”). Cognate with Dutch redden, English redd and rid.

noun:Rechen.tx: From Middle High German rëche, Old High German rëhkho. Cognate with Middle Dutch rake, Old Norse reka (“rake”), Old English racu, Dutch reek (“rake”), English rake, Gothic 𐍂𐌹𐌺𐌰𐌽 (rikan, “to heap up, collect”). From Proto-Germanic *rakō, *rekô (“rake”).

noun:Rocker.tx: From rocken + -er or Rock + -er. The "biker" sense is a pseudo-anglicism.

noun:Rechnung.tx: From rechnen + -ung. Compare Dutch rekening, English reckoning.

adj:rau.tx: From Middle High German rūch, from Old High German rūh, from Proto-Germanic *rūhwaz. Though etymologically justified, the silent h was abolished in 1996 because rauh was the only word in which it was used after the diphthong -au-. Cognate with Dutch ruig and ruw, English rough (which see).

noun:Richtung.tx: From Middle High German richtunge, from Old High German rihtunga, from Proto-West Germanic *rihtungu. By surface analysis, richten + -ung.

prep:Richtung.tx: Ellipsis of "in Richtung" (“in (the) direction (of)”). The usage with the nominative is a result of the original phrase attaching the specific direction as an apposition, leaving it uninflected.

noun:Rechenschaft.tx: From Middle High German rechinschafft, equivalent to rechnen + -schaft.

verb:rechnen.tx: From Middle High German rëchenen, from Old High German rëhhanōn (akin to Old Saxon *rekenen), from Proto-West Germanic *rekanōn. Compare Hunsrik rechne, Low German rekenen, Dutch rekenen and English reckon. Indirectly derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ-.

noun:Ross.tx: From Middle High German ros (“horse”), from Old High German ros, hros (“horse”), from Proto-West Germanic *hross.

noun:Ruß.tx: From Middle High German ruoȥ, rūȥ, from Old High German ruoȥ, hruoȥ, from Proto-Germanic *hrōtaz (“soot”), from Proto-Indo-European *kreH(u)d-.

noun:Riss.tx: From Middle High German riss, from Old High German riz, from Proto-Germanic *writiz.

verb:rühren.tx: From Middle High German rüeren, from Old High German ruoren, hruoren, from Proto-West Germanic *hrōʀijan. Cognate with Dutch roeren, now rare English rear (“to move, stir”).

noun:Rätsel.tx: From northern Middle High German rētsel, rātsel, from Old High German rādisli (10th c., hapax: ze radislen, Ripuarian), from Proto-West Germanic *rādislī. Equivalent to raten + -sel. The formation was restricted to parts of Central German and was later reinforced by Middle Low German rēdesal, rēdelse. It established itself in the standard language after Luther’s usage. Upper German synonyms were …

verb:raten.tx: From Middle High German rāten, from Old High German rātan, from Proto-West Germanic *rādan, from Proto-Germanic *rēdaną. Cognate with Low German raden, Dutch raden, English rede, read, Danish råde.

verb:räumen.tx: From Early New High German reumen, a Central German umlaut variant of the regular form raumen, from Middle High German rūmen, from Old High German rūmen, from Proto-West Germanic *rūmijan, from Proto-Germanic *rūmijaną. By surface analysis, Raum + -en. Raumen was in use in Upper German regions up until the 17th century and is still present in dialects, compare Bavarian rama.

noun:Rübe.tx: From Middle High German rüebe, ruobe, from Old High German ruoba, from Proto-West Germanic *rōbijā. Cognate with Middle Dutch roeve, Middle Low German rö̂ve (modern Rööv). Forms with back vowel in Upper German dialects are due to umlaut hindrance before labials, but Icelandic rófa, Danish roe, Swedish rova require a byform Proto-Germanic *rōbǭ. See also Latin rāpa, rāpum, Proto-Slavic *rěpa, …

noun:Rabe.tx: From Middle High German rabe, from Old High German rabo, from Proto-West Germanic *hrabō, from Proto-Germanic *hrabô, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂-. See also Proto-Germanic *hrabnaz. Compare Low German Raav, Dutch raaf, West Frisian, English raven, Danish ravn.

noun:Roggen.tx: From a German Low German form of classical Rocken.

noun:Rebhuhn.tx: From Middle High German rëphuon, from Old High German rebhuon, rebahuon, cognate to or adapted from Proto-Slavic *arębъ (“partridge”) + Huhn.

noun:Rampe.tx: Borrowed from French rampe, from Old French ramper, ultimatively from Proto-Germanic *hrimpaną (“to bend, curve, make waves, wrinkle”), whence German rümpfen. Possibly a doublet of Rumpf. Compare English ramp.

noun:Ranke.tx: From Middle High German ranke, from Old High German hranca.

noun:Ranzen.tx: From Middle High German rans (“belly, paunch, satchel”), 15th century thieves' cant. From the same root as Swedish ränsel and Dutch ransel.

noun:Rasen.tx: From north-eastern Middle High German rase, probably from Middle Low German wrāse (“sod, turf”), though the two could also be cognate forms. Further origin presumably a variant of Middle Low German wāse, from Old Saxon waso, from Proto-West Germanic *wasō (“moisture, slime, muck”) which has been inherited as German Wasen. The intermitting r might be due to influence from dialectal forms of Brodem …

noun:Rast.tx: From Middle High German raste, from Old High German rasta.

noun:Rede.tx: From Middle High German rede, from Old High German redia, radia (“speech, view, opinion”), from Proto-Germanic *raþjǭ, *raþjō (“accountability, speech”); from the same root as reden (“to talk, to speak”). Cognate with Latin ratiō (“account, reason, proof”) and German Rat (“counsel”), English rede (“counsel”).

noun:Regel.tx: From Middle High German rëgel, from Old High German rëgula, from Proto-West Germanic *regulu, from Latin regula (“rule”).

noun:Reh.tx: From Middle High German rē, rēch, from Old High German rēh, rēho, from Proto-West Germanic *raih, from Proto-Germanic *raihô, *raihą. More at roe.

verb:reiben.tx: From Middle High German rīben, from Old High German rīban, from Proto-West Germanic *wrīban. Cognate with Hunsrik reive, Dutch wrijven, Alemannic German riibe. Compare English ribald.

noun:Reif.tx: From Middle High German rīf(e), from Old High German rīfo, hrīfo, from Proto-West Germanic *hrīpō. Cognate with Dutch rijp. Likely related with (and possibly from a stem variant of) Proto-Germanic *hrīmô, whence English rime.

noun:Reihe.tx: From Middle High German rīhe, from Old High German *rīha, from Proto-West Germanic *rīhu, *rīgu, akin to Old High German riga. More at row.

noun:Reim.tx: From Middle High German rīm m (“rhyme”). In form probably inherited from Old High German rīm m (“number, count, series”), from Proto-West Germanic *rīm, from Proto-Germanic *rīmą. However, the sense follows Old French rime f (“rhyme”), whose origin is uncertain: either from the same Germanic noun or from Latin rhythmus. In the latter case, a doublet of Rhythmus.

noun:Reue.tx: From Middle High German riuwe, from Old High German riuwa, from Proto-West Germanic *hreuwu. Cognate with English rue through Old English hrēow.

noun:Riegel.tx: From Middle High German rigel, from Old High German rigil, of unclear derivation, either related to words like Reihe (Reige), Reck, regen, or borrowed from Latin rēgula. Cognate to Dutch richel, Vilamovian rejgel.

noun:Riemen.tx: From Middle High German rieme, from Old High German riomo, from Proto-West Germanic *reumō. Because of its superficial similarity to Russian ремень (remenʹ), some early Russian dictionaries posited a connection between the words, either deriving the Slavic one from the Germanic one (as Chudinov did), or deriving the Germanic word from the Slavic one (as Dal did). The latter suggestion is …

noun:Riff.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German rif, ref, from Old Norse rif.

noun:Rille.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Rille, from Middle Low German *rille, probably an old diminutive of rīde (“little stream”), itself from Proto-Germanic *rīþaz (“river”), in spite of late attestations. Compare Dutch ril, English rill.

noun:Rinne.tx: From Middle High German rinne, from Old High German rinna, from Proto-Germanic *rinnǭ.

noun:Rippe.tx: From Middle High German rippe (also ruppe, ribbe, ribe, riebe), from Old High German rippa, ribba, (also rippi, ribbi), from Proto-West Germanic *ribi, from Proto-Germanic *ribją (“rib, reef”). Cognate with English rib, Dutch rib (“rib”), Low German ribbe (“rib”), Old Norse rif (“rib, reef”).

verb:ritzen.tx: From Middle High German ritzen, *rizzen (in combinations), from the fusion of Old High German rizzen (from Proto-West Germanic *rittjan (“to tear, cut”)) and Old High German rizzōn, rezzōn (“to scratch; tear; cut; incise”) (from riz (“scoring; crack; incision; impression; stroke; character, letter”)). Compare Middle Low German ritten (“to tear, rip, rupture, nick”), Middle English ritten (“to …

noun:Ruck.tx: From Middle High German ruc, from Old High German rucch, ultimately from the root of rücken (“to rock, push, move”).

noun:Ruder.tx: From Middle High German ruoder, from Old High German ruoder, ruodar, from Proto-West Germanic *rōþr. Compare Dutch roer, English rudder.

noun:Rüge.tx: Inherited from Middle High German rüege. Cognate with Old English wrōht, Gothic 𐍅𐍂𐍉𐌷𐍃 (wrōhs).

noun:Ruhe.tx: From Middle High German ruo, ruowe, from Old High German ruowa (“peace, quiet, rest”), from Proto-West Germanic *rōu (“calm, rest”).

noun:Ruhm.tx: From Middle High German ruom, from Old High German ruom, from Proto-West Germanic *hrōmi, from Proto-Germanic *hrōmiz.

noun:Rumpf.tx: From Middle High German rumph, perhaps ultimately related to rümpfen (“to wrinkle”). See English rump for more.

noun:Runzel.tx: From Middle High German runzel, from Old High German runzula, runzila, a diminutive of Proto-West Germanic *hrunkwitā (“wrinkle”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kreng-, from a nasalized form of Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerg-, from a phonetic extension of Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”). Compare Old Norse hrukka (“wrinkle”), Swedish rynka (“wrinkle”).

verb:rüsten.tx: From Middle High German rüsten, from Old High German rusten, hrusten (“prepare, adorn”) (8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *hrustijan, cognate with Old English hyrstan (“equip, adorn”), root-cognate with Greek κρύπτω (krúptō, “cover, conceal”).

noun:Riesling.tx: Uncertain. Possibly from a Middle High German variant of rueszling, perhaps ruoz (“soot”), from Old High German hruoz, from Proto-Germanic *hrōtaz (“soot”) + the suffix -ling. The semantic connection with soot would be referring to the grapes' tendency to develop black spots when ripe. There are several written references to the variety of grape dating from the 15th century.

noun:Rocken.tx: From Middle High German rocke, from Old High German rocko, from Proto-West Germanic *rokkō, from Proto-Germanic *rukkô.

adj:rund.tx: From Middle High German runt, from Old French ront, from Latin rotundus (“round”) from rota (“wheel, disk”).

adv:rund.tx: From Middle High German runt, from Old French ront, from Latin rotundus (“round”) from rota (“wheel, disk”).

verb:rasen.tx: An originally Central and Low German verb, from Middle High German rāsen and Middle Low German rāsen, from Proto-West Germanic *rāsijan (“to race, rush”). Cognates include: Dutch razen, Old English rǣsan (“to hurry”), Old Norse rása (“to move quickly”).

verb:reichen.tx: From Middle High German reichen, from Old High German reihhen, reichen, from Proto-West Germanic *raikijan, from Proto-Germanic *raikijaną. Compare Dutch reiken, English reach.

verb:roden.tx: From northern Middle High German roten, roden and Middle Low German rōden, from Proto-Germanic *rudōną, which is related to *raupijaną (“to rip out, pluck”), *reufaną (“to tear”). Cognate with Dutch rooien. Also akin to English rid, Danish rydde. The variant rotten (still in ausrotten) shows a more southern phonetical development. However, most Upper German dialects used the verb reuten, from Old …

noun:Retter.tx: From Late Middle High German rettære; cf. German retten.

noun:Rechteck.tx: recht (“right”) + Eck (“angle”); calque of Latin rēctangulum.

verb:reinigen.tx: From Middle High German reinegen, reinigen, synchronically analyzed as a verbal derivative of rein (“pure, clean”). Cognate with English rinse.

noun:Rubin.tx: Borrowed from Latin rubīnus, from ruber (“red”).

noun:Reklame.tx: Borrowed from French réclame. Cognate with English reclaim.

noun:Radieschen.tx: Diminutive of earlier Radies, borrowed from Dutch radijs, itself from Middle French radice, from Italian radice, from Latin rādīx.

noun:Rhabarber.tx: From Italian rabarbaro, from Latin rhabarbarum, reubarbarum, from Ancient Greek ῥῆον βαρβαρικόν (rhêon barbarikón).

noun:Roboter.tx: Since 1922, derived from Czech robot, in part through English robot. The Czech was coined by Karel Čapek from robota (“serfdom”), whence come also German Robot (“serfdom”), roboten (“to work as serf, toil”). In fact, Middle High German already had a noun robater (“serf”), but this was not continued. It is possible, however, that the German translator derived Roboter from the verb roboten + -er …

adj:ruchlos.tx: From Middle High German ruochlōs, ruochelōs, rūchelōs, from Old High German ruochalōs, ruohhalōs, from Proto-Germanic *rōkōlausaz, *rōkijalausaz, cognate with English reckless.

noun:Rakete.tx: Borrowed from Italian rocchetta, diminutive of rocca (“distaff”). Compare the Icelandic raketta (“a skyrocket, a rocket”).

noun:Referat.tx: From Latin referat (“may he tell!”), third-person singular present subjunctive of referō.

noun:Reptil.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin reptilis (“creeping”), from Latin rēpō (“to creep”).

adj:ruhig.tx: From Middle High German ruowec (“quiet”). By surface analysis, Ruhe + -ig.

adv:ruhig.tx: From Middle High German ruowec (“quiet”). By surface analysis, Ruhe + -ig.

adj:rentabel.tx: Mid-19th century, from Rente + -abel. French rentable is not attested before the late 19th century.

noun:Rüstung.tx: 16th century, from rüsten + -ung. Old High German had hrust (“armour”), but this was ousted in Middle High German by different lexemes such as panzier, harnasch. Old High German hrustunga is morphologically identical but had a general meaning of “installation, trappings” and remained without continuation.

noun:Radler.tx: Radler is a Bavarian word for Radfahrer (“cyclist”): Rad + -ler. Also analysable as radeln + -er. There are several theories about the origin of the beverage and its naming, but they are all dated in the 19ᵗʰ century, when the beverage became a popular thirst quencher with lower alcoholic content than beer within the emerging movement of recreational cycling among the working class.

noun:Radfahrer.tx: From Rad (“bicycle”) + Fahrer (“driver”). The former is short for Fahrrad. The figurative sense (early 20th c.) is from the notion of nach oben buckeln und nach unten treten (“to bow to the top and kick to the bottom”).

noun:Rolle.tx: 15th century, from Old French rolle, probably through Middle Dutch rolle (as also the verb rollen). Further from Latin rotula, rotulus. The sense “role” from the modern French descendant rôle.

verb:rechtfertigen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German rëhtvertegen, rëhtvertigen, from Middle High German rëhtvertec, rëhtvertic (“just, proper, righteous”), for which compare also rechtschaffen. By surface analysis, recht + fertigen.

noun:Risiko.tx: Borrowed in the 16th century from older Italian risico (contemporary rischio). Further origin unsettled.

noun:Rabbiner.tx: From Latin rabinus + -er. Doublet of Rabbi and Rebbe.

noun:Rutsche.tx: From Middle High German rütsche, deverbal from rütschen.

verb:ruinieren.tx: Borrowed from French ruiner. Equivalent to Ruine or Ruin + -ieren.

noun:Ratsche.tx: From the verb ratschen (long a), from Middle High German ratzen (“to clatter”).

noun:Rivale.tx: Borrowed from French rival, initially as Rival (which Grimm still lists as the only form). In the 19th century, the singular was suffixed with -e, which Pfeifer suggests may have been a reanalysis a previously strong plural..

noun:Rente.tx: Borrowed from Old French rente, from Early Medieval Latin rendita.

noun:Ruhestand.tx: From Ruhe and Stand, one may think about Familienstand and Berufsstand. Sometimes it is also called ironically Unruhestand (status of no rest) if one has the feeling that one has less time than before the retirement.

verb:raufen.tx: From Middle High German roufen, from Old High German roufen, from Proto-West Germanic *raupijan.

noun:Rosine.tx: From Middle High German rosīn, *rosīne, from Middle Dutch rosīne (whence Dutch rozijn), from Picard Old French *roisine, northern variant of Old French raisin (whence also French raisin and English raisin), from Late Latin racīmus, from Latin racēmus. Within German, the word was originally chiefly Low and Central German, while Upper German dialects used the word Zibebe. It is therefore likely …

noun:Realismus.tx: From real + -ismus. Compare English realism and French réalisme.

adj:romantisch.tx: Borrowed from English romantic, from French romantique, equivalent to Romantik + -isch.

noun:Rassenhygiene.tx: Coined by German physician Alfred Ploetz in 1895, equivalent to Rasse (“race”) + Hygiene (“hygiene”)

noun:Reißverschluss.tx: From reißen (“to pull apart, tear”) + Verschluss (“closure, shutter”).

noun:Rhesusaffe.tx: From French rhésus + Affe (“ape, monkey”), partial calque of French singe rhésus.

noun:Rosenkohl.tx: Rose + -n- + Kohl. Named after the rose-shaped vegetable part (part which is consumed as a vegetable).

noun:Rüde.tx: From Middle High German rüde, rüd, from Old High German rudio, from Proto-Germanic *hruþjô (“male dog”), possibly from *hruttōn- (“to roar”), from a Proto-Indo-European root shared by Ancient Greek κόρυζα (kóruza), Old English hrot. Or, from Proto-Germanic *hreutan-, *hrūtan-, *hruttōną (“to snore”), which would be related to Old Norse hrjóta. Cognate to Dutch reu, probably also to Low German Rühe (“dog”).

verb:rotzen.tx: From Proto-Germanic *hruttōną (“to snore, roar”), attested since the 16th century, synchronically analyzable as Rotz + -en.

noun:Razzia.tx: Mid-19th century, from French razzia, from Algerian Arabic غزية (ḡazya), from Classical Arabic غَزْوة (ḡazwa, “military raid, foray”). Adopted with a spelling pronunciation, perhaps after Italian borrowings with -zz- like Skizze or Intermezzo.

noun:Regenwurm.tx: From Middle High German regenwurm, from Old High German reganwurm, from Proto-West Germanic *regnawurmi. Analysable as Regen (“rain”) + Wurm (“worm”), so called because of the animal’s habit of surfacing after rainfall. Cognate with Old English reġnwyrm, whence English rainworm.

noun:Räson.tx: Borrowed from French raison. Doublet of Ratio, Ration, and Rede.

noun:Rezept.tx: From earlier Recept, recept, from Latin receptus, thus cognate with English receipt.

noun:Raumfahrt.tx: Raum (“space”) + fahren (“to go by vehicle, drive”).

noun:Rektorin.tx: From Rektor + -in, from Latin rēctor. Compare feminine rēctrīx.

noun:Rechenbrett.tx: the root of rechnen 'to calculate' + Brett 'board, slate'

noun:Redensart.tx: From Reden + -s + Art, a calque of French façon de parler. Cognate to Low German Rädensoarten (plural).

adv:runter.tx: Contraction of herunter (“down here”), semantically influenced by hinunter (“down there”).

verb:rasieren.tx: 17th century, from French raser, from Old French raser, from Vulgar Latin *rāsāre.

noun:R-Gespräch.tx: Shortened from Rückwärtsberechnungsgespräch (literally “reverse-charge call”); originally a trade name introduced by Deutsche Telekom.

noun:Rochen.tx: From Middle Low German roche, ruche, possibly a derivative of Proto-Germanic *rūhwaz (“rough”), but often thought to be from a substrate (compare also Latin raia). Cognate with Dutch rog, Old English reohhe, ruhha, and, via Old French, English roach (“a fish”).

verb:rülpsen.tx: Uncertain. Usually regarded as imitative (lautmalend). Compare Middle Low German ruspelen (“to burp, regurgitate, vomit”), Middle High German rüspeln, riuspeln ("to clear one's throat"; > German räuspeln, räuspern), Old High German girūspen (“to resist, struggle up”).

verb:renovieren.tx: Borrowed from Middle French renover (modern French rénover), from Latin renovō.

noun:Ressentiment.tx: Borrowed from French ressentiment, from an archaic usage of the verb ressentir, via Old French sentir from Latin sentiō, sentīre (“to feel”).

noun:Rhetorik.tx: From Middle High German rhetorica/retorica, from Latin rhētorica, from Ancient Greek ῥητορικός (rhētorikós). Compare French rhétorique.

noun:Regisseur.tx: Borrowed from French régisseur, which stands for bailiff or trustee in English, as well as assistant director in theater. The word is actually a false friend; in French the film director is a metteur en scène or sometimes réalisateur, but never a régisseur.

verb:reformieren.tx: From Latin reformo. Cognate with Hunsrik rëformeere.

noun:Reportage.tx: Borrowed from French reportage. Analysable as Report + -age.

noun:Ressource.tx: Borrowed from French ressource, since the 18th century.

adj:rosig.tx: Inherited from Middle High German rōsic. By surface analysis, Rose + -ig.

noun:Rädelsführer.tx: Cognate with Bavarian Rädel (“small circle of persons, ranks, dancing-song”).

verb:ratifizieren.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ratificare, from Latin ratus (“established, authoritative; fixed, certain”) + faciō, facere (“to make”)

verb:rauschen.tx: From Middle High German rūschen (also riuschen), from Old High German *rūskōn, from Proto-West Germanic *rūskōn, from Proto-Germanic *rūskōną (“to storm, whiz, make a noise”). Cognate with Dutch ruisen and, possibly, with English rush (see there).

verb:regieren.tx: From Middle High German regieren, borrowed from Old French reger, from Latin regō. Cognate with Hunsrik rëghiere.

noun:Rettung.tx: From Middle High German rettunge, equivalent to retten + -ung.

adj:rasant.tx: 18th century, borrowed from French rasant in the military sense. The sense “rapid” through influence by unrelated German rasen (“to rush”).

verb:referenzieren.tx: Borrowed from French référencer. By surface analysis, Referenz + -ieren.

noun:Rekrut.tx: Borrowed from Middle French recrute (attested 1592), from recreue (“supplement”), recrue (“supplies; supplemental soldiers”) (attested 1550), substantivized past participle of Old French recroistre (“to grow again, to acquire offspring, to replace”), from Latin recrēscere (“to grow (out) again”).

noun:Römer.tx: From Middle High German Rœmer, Rœmære, Rômære. Equivalent to Rom + -er.

adj:Römer.tx: From Middle High German Rœmer, Rœmære, Rômære. Equivalent to Rom + -er.

noun:Röntgen.tx: From etymology 2, the surname of the inventor.

verb:rutschen.tx: From an onomatopoeic Middle High German rutzen, rützen (whence also the obsolete form rütschen), with change of -tz- to -tsch- as also in fletschen. Perhaps related to Old High German rūtezzen. English rutch and rutsch derive from this term or its cognates in related languages.

adj:rostig.tx: From Middle High German rostec, from Old High German rostag, from Proto-Germanic *rustagaz (“rusty”), equivalent to Rost (“rust”) + -ig (“-y”). Cognate with English rusty.

noun:Ration.tx: 18th century, from French ration. Doublet of Räson, Ratio, and Rede.

verb:regulieren.tx: From Middle High German [Term?]. Cognate with Hunsrik rëguleere.

verb:realisieren.tx: Borrowed from French réaliser. Compare Hunsrik rëaliseere. The sense “to become aware of” is a semantic loan from English realize.

verb:rechten.tx: From Middle High German rehten, from Old High German rehton.

verb:rächen.tx: From Middle High German rëchen, from Old High German rëhhan, wrëhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrekan, from Proto-Germanic *wrekaną. Cognate with Dutch wreken, English wreak.

noun:Roch.tx: From Middle High German roch, from Arabic رُخّ (ruḵḵ), from Middle Persian lhw'. The /x/ must be compared to the word Schach. In both of these cases it is either due to direct borrowing from Arabic (during the Crusades) or alternatively to borrowing via Middle Dutch roc, from Old French roc, with artificial application of the High German consonant shift.

noun:Raubtier.tx: From rauben (“to steal, prey upon”) + Tier (“animal”).

verb:rücken.tx: From Middle High German rücken, Old High German rucchen, from Proto-West Germanic *rukkijan. Cognate with Old Norse rykkja, Old English roccian, English rock.

adj:rasch.tx: From Middle High German rasch, rasche, from Old High German reski, rasco (adverb). Cognate with Swedish rask, Danish rask, English rash; see the latter for more.

adv:rasch.tx: From Middle High German rasch, rasche, from Old High German reski, rasco (adverb). Cognate with Swedish rask, Danish rask, English rash; see the latter for more.

adj:religiös.tx: From Latin religiōsus, with assimilation to native suffix -ös (ultimately of French origin).

noun:Runde.tx: From rund + -e. Certain senses influenced by French ronde.

noun:Reiter.tx: From Middle High German rîter, rîtære, from Old High German rîtari. Not of Proto-Germanic age, but an OHG formation from the verb rītan "to ride" (Anglo-Saxon rîdere and Old Icelandic ríðari are loans from OHG). Low German has riddere, with short vowel and geminate. Middle High German forms seem to have varied between long and short vowel, riter vs. rîter respectively, the latter giving rise to …

noun:Redner.tx: From Middle High German redenære, from Old High German redināri, derived from the verb redinōn, a lost byform of redōn (whence reden). Now analysable as reden + -ner.

noun:Ruhr.tx: From Late Latin rubro gilum (“red brook”), of Celtic origin; for the second element see the river Celbis.

noun:Raspel.tx: 16th century, back-formation from raspeln, which see.

noun:Reißbrett.tx: reißen + Brett. Compare also English write (“to inscribe, engrave, imprint”) + board. The older meaning of reißen refers to the consequences of using a tool for engraving or drawing, causing little cracks on a surface of choice, which, among other things, could also have been used as means of writing.

noun:Rikscha.tx: Borrowed from English rickshaw or its source, Japanese 力(りき)車(しゃ) (rikisha).

noun:Raumzeit.tx: A dvandva compound of Raum (“space”) + Zeit (“time”). Coined by German mathematician and physicist Hermann Minkowski.

verb:ringen.tx: From Middle High German ringen, from Old High German ringan, from Proto-West Germanic *wringan, from Proto-Germanic *wringaną. Cognate with wringen (from Low German), English wring, and Dutch wringen.

verb:ruhen.tx: From Middle High German ruo(we)n, from Old High German ruowēn. See Ruhe (“rest”).

noun:Raute.tx: From Middle High German rūte, from Old High German rūta, from Proto-West Germanic *rūtā (“rue”).

verb:ramponieren.tx: 18th c., from Low German, from Middle Low German ramponēren, from Middle Dutch ramponeren (whence Dutch rampeneren), from Old French ramposner (“to taunt”), of uncertain derivation. The semantic development under influence of Middle Dutch ramp (“harm, calamity, catastrophe”).

verb:reisen.tx: From Middle High German reisen, from Old High German reisōn, from Proto-West Germanic *raisōn, further from Proto-West Germanic *raisu (akin to Proto-Germanic *raizijaną).

noun:Recke.tx: From Middle High German reche, from Old High German reccho, from Proto-West Germanic *wrakkjō, from Proto-Germanic *wrakjô.

verb:recken.tx: From Middle High German recken, from Old High German recchen, from Proto-West Germanic *rakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *rakjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃roǵéyeti.

noun:Rechtschreibung.tx: Late 16th or early 17th century calque of Latin ortographia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθογρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (orthogrăphĭ́ā); compare Old High German rehtscrībāri (“person who writes correctly”), itself a calque of Latin orthographus. By surface analysis, recht (“proper, correct”) + Schreibung (“spelling”)

noun:Reichtum.tx: From Middle High German rīchtuom, from Old High German rīhhituom, rīhtuom, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijadōmaz, equivalent to reich + -tum. Cognate with Hunsrik Reichdum, Dutch rijkdom, English richdom.

verb:reparieren.tx: Borrowed from Latin reparō. Compare to English repair.

noun:Restauration.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin restaurātiōnem. First attested in the 16th century.

noun:Raumfähre.tx: From Raum (“space”) + Fähre (“ferry”). Attested since at least 1962.

verb:rudern.tx: From Middle High German ruodern, from Old High German ruoderōn, garuoderōn, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *rōaną (“to row”). Also see Ruder.

noun:Ramsch.tx: Uncertain, perhaps related to Etymology 2. Possibly cognate with Dutch ramsj, from Yiddish ראַמש (ramsh).

noun:Realpolitik.tx: From real (“real”) + Politik (“politics”), introduced by August Ludwig von Rochau.

verb:reimen.tx: From Middle High German rīmen (“to compose, put into verse, rhyme”), from Old High German rīman (“to count, enumerate”), from Proto-Germanic *rīmaną (“to count”). Cognate with Middle Low German rîmen (“to appraise, show honour, put into verse, rhyme”).

noun:Radix.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin rādīx (“root”). Doublet of Rettich.

verb:reuen.tx: From a merger of: * Middle High German riuwen (strong declension), from Old High German riuwan, hriuwan, from Proto-West Germanic *hreuwan, from Proto-Germanic *hrewwaną; and * Middle High German riuwen (weak declension), itself a merger from Old High German riuwēn, from Proto-West Germanic *hriuwjan, from Proto-Germanic *hriuwjan; and Old High German riuwōn, hriuwōn, from Proto-West Germanic …

verb:rinnen.tx: From Middle High German rinnen, from Old High German rinnan, from Proto-West Germanic *rinnan.

noun:Rechtsstaat.tx: Coined by Carl Theodor Welcker in 1813, equivalent to Recht + -s- + Staat. Popularized by Robert von Mohl.

noun:Regent.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin rēgēns (genitive singular rēgentis).

noun:Reling.tx: From Low German Reling, Regeling, derived from Middle Low German rēgel, from Old Saxon *rigil, probably from Latin regula, though this sometimes doubted. Cognate with German Riegel, Dutch richel, and possibly English rail. The form Reling was reinforced and standardised under the influence of English railing.

verb:reflektieren.tx: Borrowed from Latin reflectere. Compare Hunsrik rëfletiere, which has been influenced by Portuguese.

noun:Resultat.tx: Borrowed from French résultat, from Medieval Latin resultātum, the substantivized neuter singular of resultātus (perfect passive participle of resultō). By surface analysis, resultieren + -at.

noun:Randale.tx: Originally plural of now obsolete Randal (“noise, tumult”). Pseudo-Latinism, derived from a humorous pseudo-Latin formation from dialectal Rand (“noise, ballyhoo”) to rhyme with Skandal (“scandal”) and possibly also Vandal(e) (“vandal”).

noun:Regentropfen.tx: From Middle High German regentropfe, from Old High German regantropfo, from Proto-Germanic *regnadrupô. Equivalent to Regen + Tropfen.

noun:Rochade.tx: 19th century, from rochieren + -ade, after French rocade.

verb:rügen.tx: From Middle High German rüegen, from Old High German ruogen, from Proto-Germanic *wrōgijaną.

noun:Reet.tx: Borrowed from Low German Reet, from Middle Low German rêt, from Old Saxon hriod, from Proto-West Germanic *hreud.

adv:rechtens.tx: Equivalent to recht (“right, correct, just”) + -ens (adverbial suffix).

conj:respektive.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin respectīvē, adverb of respectīvus.

noun:Rinnsal.tx: From rinnen (“to trickle”) + -sal (abstract noun suffix). Possibly from Proto-Germanic *rannislō and cognate with Icelandic rennsli (“run, leak”).

noun:Rammler.tx: From late Middle High German rammeler, remler. By surface analysis, rammeln (“to copulate”) + -er (agent noun suffix). Cognate of Dutch rammelaar.

noun:Regenpfeifer.tx: From Regen + Pfeifer. Compare Bulgarian дъждосви́рец (dăždosvírec).

noun:Reede.tx: Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German rēde, akin to Plautdietsch reed (“ready”), from Old Saxon *girēdi, from Proto-West Germanic *(ga)raidī, from Proto-Germanic *raidaz.

noun:Rösti.tx: Borrowed from Alemannic German, from the same root as rösten (“to roast, to toast”).

noun:Revier.tx: Inherited from Middle High German riviere (“undeveloped area; hunting ground; river”), borrowed, probably through Middle Dutch riviere (“river; riverside used for hunting birds”), from Old French riviere (“idem”), from Latin riparia (“riverside”). Cognate with modern Dutch rivier, English river, modern French rivière. The use as a proper noun goes back to the now-archaic designation …

noun:Rüsche.tx: Borrowed from French ruche, from Middle French rusche, from Old French rusche, from Early Medieval Latin rusca (“bark”), borrowed from Gaulish rūsca, from Proto-Celtic *rūskos (“bark”), from *rukskos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rewk- (“to dig up”), from *Hrew- (“to tear out, dig out”).

verb:rosten.tx: From Middle High German rosten, from Old High German rostēn. Equivalent to Rost + -en.

noun:Rücksicht.tx: 18th century calque of Latin respectus. Equivalent to rück- + Sicht.

adj:rudimentär.tx: Borrowed from French rudimentaire, from French rudiment, from Latin rudimentum.

adj:rastlos.tx: Equivalent to Rast + -los. Cognate to English restless, Dutch rusteloos.

noun:Rauke.tx: 16th century, from dialectal Italian ruca, from Latin ērūca. In the 15th century also erucke (and variants), perhaps from another Romance source or directly from Latin. The herb was little used in German cuisine until the 1980s, when in the course of marketing changes also the synonym Rucola appeared.

noun:Rabatt.tx: From now-archaic Italian rabbatto (French, Old French rabat) in the mid-17th century, deverbal from Italian rabbattere (French rabattre, Old French rabatre). These verbs suggest a Late Latin *re-abbattere. Compare Late Latin abbattere, abattere (6th century), whose base is Late Latin battere, from Latin battuere. Cognate with English rebate.

noun:Rabatte.tx: From Dutch rabat from Middle French rabat ultimately a form of Old French rabatte. Cognate with German Rabatt

verb:rasten.tx: Inherited from Middle High German rasten, from Old High German rastōn, from Proto-West Germanic *rastōn (“to rest”), equivalent to Rast + -en. Cognate with Middle Low German rasten (“to rest”), dialectal Dutch rasten (“to rest”), Saterland Frisian räästje (“to rest”), Middle English rasten (“to rest”).

verb:rösten.tx: From Middle High German rœsten, from Old High German rōsten, from Proto-West Germanic *raustijan. By surface analysis, Rost (“grill, grid”) + -en. Related with English roast.

verb:rocken.tx: Borrowed from English rock, equivalent to Rock + -en.

verb:rezitieren.tx: Borrowed from Latin recitāre, infinitive of recitō (“to read aloud, recite”).

adj:rigoros.tx: From Medieval Latin rigorōsus influenced by French rigoureux.

verb:rekonstruieren.tx: 18th century, from re- + konstruieren, after French reconstruire.

noun:Rollo.tx: Alteration (based on rollen, Rollladen) of older Rouleau, from French rouleau.

noun:Rank.tx: From Middle High German ranc (“a quick turning movement”), from Old High German *rank, from Proto-Germanic *wrankiz (“a turn, twisting”). Cognate with English wrench.

verb:rumoren.tx: Middle High German rumōren, from Latin rumōr.

adj:reichlich.tx: From Middle High German rīch(e)lich, from Old High German rīhlīh, *rīhhilīh. By surface analysis, reich (“rich”) + -lich. In modern German it can also be reinterpreted as reichen (“to suffice”) + -lich, but this is unetymological. Cognate with Dutch rijkelijk.

adv:reichlich.tx: From Middle High German rīch(e)lich, from Old High German rīhlīh, *rīhhilīh. By surface analysis, reich (“rich”) + -lich. In modern German it can also be reinterpreted as reichen (“to suffice”) + -lich, but this is unetymological. Cognate with Dutch rijkelijk.

noun:Rabenvater.tx: Rabe (“raven”) + Vater (“father”), in analogy to Rabenmutter.

noun:Roche.tx: From Middle High German roc, from Old French roche, ultimately from Persian رخ (rox, “rook”).

noun:Ruhetag.tx: Ruhe (“rest”) + Tag (“day”), or ruhen (“to rest”) + Tag (“day”)

noun:Rande.tx: Variant of Rahne, which probably is related to the adjective rahn (“slim”).

adj:restlich.tx: From Middle High German restlich, equivalent to Rest + -lich.

noun:Runge.tx: From Middle High German runge, from Old High German hrunga, from Proto-Germanic *hrungō. Cognate with Dutch rong, English rung, Gothic 𐌷𐍂𐌿𐌲𐌲𐌰 (hrugga).

verb:ragen.tx: From Middle High German ragen, from Old High German hragēn, from Proto-West Germanic *hragōn.

noun:Regenwasser.tx: From Old High German reganwazzar, from Proto-Germanic *regnawatōr. Equivalent to Regen (“rain”) + Wasser (“water”).

verb:randalieren.tx: From Randal + -ieren. The former is an earlier variant of Randale, which see for more.

noun:Rucola.tx: Borrowed from Italian rucola, diminutive of ruca, whence already earlier German Rauke. Eventually from Latin ērūca.

noun:Raubfisch.tx: Raub + Fisch, a calque to Raubtier

noun:Rockband.tx: From Rock (“rock music”) + Band (“band”), borrowed from English rock band.

noun:Ried.tx: From Middle High German riet, from Old High German riot, hriot, from Proto-West Germanic *hreud (“reed”). Final -d instead of expected -t is due to West Central German influence (cf. Old High German ried, reid). The Low German variant Reet, in turn, has -t from generalized final devoicing, such that the dentals appear to have been “transposed” between both forms.

noun:Rendite.tx: Late 19th century, at first in Switzerland. Borrowed from Italian rendita, from Vulgar Latin *rendita, whence also the doublet Rente.

noun:Reibe.tx: 15th century, deverbal from reiben (“to rub, grate”) + -e.

noun:Reparatur.tx: Beginning of the 18th century, from Latin reparātūra (literally “things about to be repaired”).

noun:Rheumatismus.tx: Early 18th century, from Latin rheumatismus, from Ancient Greek ῥευματισμός (rheumatismós).

verb:reihen.tx: From Middle High German rīhen, from Old High German rīhan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīhan, from Proto-Germanic *rīhaną; in the sense ‘to tack, to crimp’ possibly influenced by Old High German *rīhan (attested past participle girigan), from Proto-West Germanic *wrīhan, from Proto-Germanic *wrīhaną.

noun:Reuter.tx: From Dutch ruiter (“robber; soldier; cavalryman”), from Middle Dutch ruter (“robber, looter”), from Old French routier, from rote, route, whence also German Rotte. The development from “robber” to “cavalryman” by association with Dutch rijder, ridder, German Reiter, Ritter. Later on, the word was considered a mere phonetic variant of Reiter and was accordingly discouraged by the German …

noun:Redaktion.tx: Borrowed from French rédaction. False cognate of English redaction.

noun:Revision.tx: Borrowed from French révision, from Latin revīsiō.

noun:Reisender.tx: From reisend; nominalization of the adjective reisend (“traveling”).

noun:Rhinozeros.tx: From Middle High German rinōceros, from Latin rhīnocerōs, from Ancient Greek ῥῑνόκερως (rhīnókerōs, literally “nose-horned”). The inflected forms in -rosses, -rösser are by association with unrelated Ross (“horse”); the same might also apply to the neuter gender.

noun:Rubrik.tx: From Middle High German rubrike, from Old French rubrique, from Latin rubrīca (“red ochre”), the substance used to make red letters, from ruber (“red”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-.

verb:redigieren.tx: Borrowed from French rédiger, from Latin redigō.

noun:Rehabilitation.tx: Since the 18th century, borrowed from French réhabilitation, from Medieval Latin rehabilitatio.

noun:Rotte.tx: From Middle High German rotte, from Old French rote, from Latin rupta, perfect participle of rumpo. Cognate with Middle English route, Dutch rot, English rout.

adj:reuig.tx: From Middle High German riuwec, riwec, from Old High German riuwag, hriuwag. By surface analysis, reuen + -ig.

verb:rascheln.tx: 17th century, from East Central German dialects. Ultimately onomatopoeic. Compare English rustle, Dutch ritselen.

noun:Rollbahn.tx: From rollen (“to roll”) + Bahn (“way, course, lane”).

noun:Riefe.tx: Via Low German/German Low German from Middle Low German rīve (“rake”), ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *hrīban (“to rake, scratch”). Cognate with Dutch rijf (“rake”), Old Norse hrīfa (“rake”), Old English hrīfnian.

verb:reklamieren.tx: Borrowed from French réclamer, from Latin reclāmō.

noun:Ries.tx: From Middle High German ris, from Medieval Latin rīsma, from Arabic رِزْمَة (rizma, “bundle”). Cognate with English ream.

verb:rupfen.tx: From Middle High German rupfen, ropfen, from Old High German rophōn, from Proto-West Germanic *ruppōn. Intensive form of raufen, which see for more. Related but not immediately cognate with English rip.

noun:Räumte.tx: From Low German Rüümte, from Middle Low German rūmte; perhaps also influenced by cognate Dutch ruimte. Analysable as raum (“wide”) + -te; compare geräumig. Also cognate with English roomth.

noun:Reep.tx: From Middle Low German rêp, from Old Saxon *rēp, from Proto-West Germanic *raip, from Proto-Germanic *raipą, *raipaz. Compare Reif and English rope.

noun:Rechtler.tx: Either directly from Recht + -ler or backformed from Holzrechtler, from Holzrecht + -ler.

verb:rausbringen.tx: Shortening of herausbringen (“to bring out; release”). Equivalent to raus- + bringen.

adj:redlich.tx: reden (“to talk”, verb) + -lich (“-like”, adjectival suffix), literally “talkish; tending to talk”. The verb reden can also mean that one is speaking of or revealing a truth to (someone/something), so while it literally means 'to talk', it implies in some cases that one will speak with forthcomingness or truth on a subject and not conceal it.

verb:rütteln.tx: From Middle High German rütteln, rütelen, rüteln, from rütten (“to shake”) + -eln (“frequentative suffix”), from Proto-Indo-European *kreu- (“to shake, wave around”), related to Tocharian A kru (“reed”), Tocharian B kärwats, Lithuanian krutéti (“to move”). Cognate with the first part of Old English hrēaþemūs (“bat”).

noun:Reichsapfel.tx: From Reich + -s- + Apfel. Calque of Medieval Latin pomum imperiale.

verb:raffen.tx: From Middle High German raffen, reffen, from Old High German *hraffōn (“to snatch, seize”). Cf. Dutch rapen.

noun:Römertopf.tx: From Römer + Topf, because Romans used similar pots.

noun:Rist.tx: From Middle High German rist, from Old High German rist, from Proto-Germanic *wristuz. Compare English wrist.

noun:Rotze.tx: Extended form of Rotz and/or deverbal from rotzen (itself from the former).

noun:Ricke.tx: 18th century, derived from Reh, probably on the model of Zicke (“she-goat”); compare the synonym Geiß (literally “goat”). Cognate with Middle Low German rigge (“doe, young cow”).

adj:retrograd.tx: From Latin retrōgradus, from retrō (“backwards”) + gradus (“step”).

adj:ruchbar.tx: From Ruf (“renown, reputation”, literally “call”), from Middle High German ruoft, with a change from 'f' to 'ch' influenced by German Low German [Term?]. Ultimately the same root as German Gerücht (“rumor”). Unrelated but possibly influenced in form: German ruchlos (“reckless, wicked”). Likewise unrelated is German Geruch (“reek, smell”). As parallel for the sound shift from 'f' to 'ch', compare …

adj:ruppig.tx: 18th century, from Low and Central German dialects. Deverbal from Middle Low German and northern Middle High German ruppen, roppen, cognate of rupfen (“to pluck”), which see.

adj:räudig.tx: From Middle High German riudec, rūdec, from Old High German rūdīg, hrūdīg. By surface analysis, Räude + -ig.

noun:Ringel.tx: From Middle High German ringel, ringele, from Old High German ringila, diminutive of ring; equivalent to Ring + -el. Cognate with English ringlet.

noun:Reiterei.tx: Attested since 15th century in Early New High German rewtterey.

noun:Rayon.tx: Borrowed from French rayon (“department of a store; comb (of honey)”).

noun:Ricotta.tx: Borrowed from Italian ricotta (literally “cooked again”), from Latin recocta.

noun:Rezensent.tx: From Latin recēnsens (“reviewer”), from recēnseō (“review”), from re- + cēnseō (“give an opinion”).

noun:Rotauge.tx: From rot (“red”) + Auge (“eye”). Compare Luxembourgish Routa.

verb:rucken.tx: Chiefly denominal from Ruck (“jerking movement”) + -en. Absorbed related Middle High German rucken, the Upper German form of rücken (“to shift, move in some direction”) with regular suppression of umlaut in West Germanic -ukk-.

noun:Reisig.tx: From Middle High German rīsech, from Old High German rīsahi. Compare Reis n (“shoot of plant”).

verb:rattern.tx: 17th century, from Middle Low German *rateren (modern Low German ratern), variant of rettelen, *ratelen, from a frequentative of Proto-Germanic *hratōną. Doublet of German rasseln. See English rattle for more.

verb:röten.tx: From Middle High German rœten, from Old High German rōten, from Proto-West Germanic *rodēn, from Proto-Germanic *rudāną.

verb:rappeln.tx: From Old Norse hrapa (“to fall, rush headlong, hurry, hasten”). Compare Luxembourgish rabbelen, Danish rappe (“to make haste”), Swedish rappa (“to strike, beat, rap”), English rap.

noun:Riege.tx: From German Low German and Middle Low German rīge, ultimately from a derivative of Proto-Germanic *rīgǭ (“row, line”). Cognate with Middle High German rīge (“line, row, array”). Originating from Northern Germany, Friedrich Jahn, a German gymnastics educator and nationalist, introduced this Low German term in the early 19th century.

verb:röcheln.tx: From Middle High German rücheln (“to neigh; to roar”), iterative of Middle High German rohen (“to roar; to grunt; to make noise”). Cognate with Dutch rochelen.

noun:Robot.tx: From Middle High German robāt, robāte (also robbath, robolten (dative)), from Old Czech (compare Czech robota).

verb:raunen.tx: From Middle High German rūnen, from Old High German rūnōn, from Proto-West Germanic *rūnōn, from Proto-Germanic *rūnōną.

noun:Raufasertapete.tx: From Raufaser + Tapete. Further analysable as rau (“rough, crude”) + Faser (“fibre”) + Tapete (“wallpaper”).

verb:rangeln.tx: 18th century, from Low German, from Middle Low German rangelen (“to wrestle”), iterative of rangen, byform of wrangen (“to struggle”). Cognate with English wrangle. Related with German ringen (“to wring one's hands”), auswringen (“wring out”), from Proto-Germanic *wringaną. The irregular loss of initial w- in Middle Low German is due to influence by ringen (“to wrestle”), which is from a totally …

noun:Reisetasche.tx: reisen (“to travel”) + Tasche (“bag”); cognate with Hunsrik Reestasch.

phrase:Raider heißt jetzt Twix.tx: From an advertising slogan for the Twix chocolate bar: "Raider heißt jetzt Twix, sonst ändert sich nix".

verb:rühmen.tx: From Middle High German rüehmen, from Old High German ruomen, from Proto-West Germanic *hrōmijan.

noun:Rah.tx: In the nautical sense (17th c.) from Middle Low German râ, raa, from Proto-Germanic *rahō, *raihô. The spellings in -h, -he may have been influenced by dialectal continuations of cognate Middle High German rahe (“pole, bar”), from Old High German raha; though the insertion of -h- in hiatus or at the end of a vocalic stem is also a general practice in German orthography. Further cognate with Dutch ra, Old Norse rá.

noun:Ratatouille.tx: Borrowed from French ratatouille, from Occitan ratatolha.

noun:Retourkutsche.tx: retour (“return”) + Kutsche (“carriage”). In 18th century originally a hired coach whose fare included the empty return trip. Figurative meaning attested from middle of 19th century. Became a nickname for the quadriga statue on the Brandenburg Gate, which was brought to Paris by Napoleon, then returned to Berlin after his defeat.

verb:rammeln.tx: From Middle High German rammeln, from Old High German rammalōn, remmilōn. By surface analysis, Ramme (“ram”) + -eln (iterative verbal suffix).

noun:Ramme.tx: From Middle High German ramme, from Old High German ramma (“battering ram”), from rammo (“ram, male sheep”) (whence now obsolete Ramm) from the similar shape of a ram's head, from Proto-Germanic *rammaz. See also Rammbock and Rammel.

verb:ratschen.tx: Possibly identical with etymology 2, from the sound of fabric being torn in two.

noun:Rabauke.tx: Borrowed from Low German Rabauke, diminutive of Rabau (“rogue, scoundrel”), from Dutch rabauw, from Middle Dutch rabaut, from Old French ribaut. See ribald

verb:rumsen.tx: rums + -en, the first element being an onomatopoeia used to describe the impact of something dropping.

noun:Rauchverbot.tx: Rauch (“smoke”) + Verbot (“ban”). Compare Dutch rookverbod, Swedish rökförbud, Danish rygeforbud.

noun:Raster.tx: Borrowed from Latin rāster, from rāstrum (“rake”, noun), 19th c.

verb:rümpfen.tx: From Middle High German rümpfen, from Old High German (h)rimpfan, from Proto-West Germanic *hrimpan, from Proto-Germanic *hrimpaną (“to wrinkle”).

verb:rädern.tx: From Middle High German rederen. By surface analysis, Rad + -ern.

noun:Revoluzzer.tx: Duden posits an outright borrowing from Italian rivoluzionario in the 19th century, Pfeifer says it was a pejorative modification of Revolutionär with influence by the Italian term, while Kluge does not specify. In either case, the final syllables have been clipped in the process.

verb:reinfeiern.tx: From rein- + feiern, literally “to celebrate into”.

noun:Reigen.tx: Borrowed in the 19th century from Middle High German reige, an alternative form of reie, itself perhaps a borrowing of Old French raie; replaced inherited Reihen.

noun:Räucherwerk.tx: From räuchern (“to fumigate, cure”) + Werk (“work, product, implement”).

verb:raspeln.tx: 16th century, iterative of now obsolete raspen, from Middle High German raspen (“to grab, rake”), from Old High German (h)raspōn (“to rake, gather”), from Proto-West Germanic *hraspōn, from Proto-Germanic *hraspōną. This verb was, however, infrequent in Middle High German and did not have the specific sense of “rasp, grate”. Its later use seems to have been influenced by Middle French rasper (“to …

noun:Rattenfänger.tx: From Ratte (“rat”) + -n- + Fänger (“catcher”). Sense 3 from the folk tale Der Rattenfänger von Hameln ("The Pied Piper of Hamelin").

noun:Raufe.tx: Inherited from Middle High German roufe, related to raufen (“to pluck”).

verb:rieseln.tx: From Middle High German riselen, from an iterative form of Old High German rīsan (“to fall”), related to Reise (“trip, journey”) and equivalent to Middle High German risen + -eln.

verb:rechen.tx: From Middle High German rëchen, from Old High German rëhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *rekan, from Proto-Germanic *rekaną.

noun:Rohrdommel.tx: From Middle High German rōrtumel, rōrtrumel, from Old High German *rōredumbil, the second element imitative of its mating call, and the first element from Rohr (“pipe, cane, reeds”). The name underwent extensive folk-etymological reshaping; compare Old High German horotumil, with horo (“mud, slime”), and Old English rāradumbla, whose first element was associated with rārian (“to roar, cry out”).

noun:Racker.tx: From Low German Racker (“privy cleaner”, also “scoundrel”), from racken (“to scrape, sweep”).

noun:Rothaut.tx: Calque of English redskin, from rot (“red”) + Haut (“skin”).

noun:Raffzahn.tx: raffen (“to grab, grasp, snatch up”) + Zahn (“tooth”). The word, in its first sense, is an inherited word whose oldest attested form so far is Late Middle High German reffzan “incisor” that originally might have applied the probable sense “carnassial, fang; tusk”. The extension to human teeth developed probably by comparison for instance with a tusk. From 1800 onwards the word then also applied …

noun:Reff.tx: Borrowed from Low German Reff, from Middle Low German ref. Cognate with Dutch reef, English reef, Danish rev. Further origin uncertain. The West Germanic forms are possibly borrowed from Old Norse rif. If so, the word may identical to that for “rib” (Proto-Germanic *ribją), from which is also German Riff (“reef, bank of rocks”); or it may be a derivation from Old Norse ríva (“to tear”), from Proto-Germanic *rīfaną.

verb:reffen.tx: Circa 1700, from Low German reffen, derived from Middle Low German ref. See Reff for more.

noun:Rarität.tx: Borrowed from Middle French rarité (cognate with French rareté), from Latin rāritātem.

noun:Radfahren.tx: From the verb Rad fahren (“to cycle”).

noun:Reinheitsgebot.tx: From Reinheit (“purity”) + Gebot (“commandment, order, decree”). First used in the 19th century.

noun:Raubmord.tx: From Raub (“robbery”) + Mord (“murder”). Compare Dutch roofmoord.

noun:Rotlichtviertel.tx: Calque of English red-light district, Rotlicht + Viertel.

verb:renken.tx: From Middle High German renken, from Old High German *renken, from Proto-West Germanic *wrankijan. Cognate with English wrench.

noun:Renke.tx: From Middle High German renke, from rīnanke, from Rīn (“Rhine”) + anke (“trout”).

noun:Remmidemmi.tx: Unknown. At least in part, probably from Arabic رَمَضان (ramaḍān). Compare French ramdam, Italian Rabadan (“carnival in Bellinzona”).

noun:Rochus.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish [script needed] (rochus), from Hebrew ברוגז (“angry”).

noun:Rotunda.tx: Borrowed from Latin rotunda, from rotundus. Doublet of Rotunde.

noun:Rommé.tx: Pseudo-Gallicism, derived from English rummy + French -é.

noun:Rüste.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German rüste. Cognate with Dutch rust. Ablaut variant of German Rast, English rest.

noun:Rohdaten.tx: Calque of English raw data, roh + Daten.

noun:Rassel.tx: From rasseln. Cognate to English rattle.

noun:Räude.tx: From Middle High German riude, rūde, from Old High German rūda, rūdī, from Proto-West Germanic *hrūþu, from Proto-Germanic *hrūþō (“scab, mange”). Cognate with Dutch rui (“moulting”), Old English hrūþe (“itch, rash, mange”).

noun:Rheuma.tx: Early 18th century, from Latin rheuma, from Ancient Greek ῥεῦμα (rheûma).

noun:Räuberei.tx: From Middle High German rouberīe. By surface analysis, rauben + -erei.

verb:rumpeln.tx: From Middle High German rumpeln, from Middle Low German rumpelen, ultimately onomatopoeic iteratives.

adj:raum.tx: From Middle High German rūm, from Old Saxon *rūmo, from Proto-West Germanic *rūm (“spacious, roomy”).

noun:Rückbesinnung.tx: From rückbesinnen + -ung, equivalent to rück- + Besinnung.

verb:rechtschreiben.tx: Back-formation from Rechtschreibung (“orthography”). By surface analysis, recht (“proper, correct”) + schreiben (“to spell”).

noun:Rodung.tx: From roden (“to clear”) + -ung (“-ing”). Compare Old English hryding (“clearing, cleared land”).

noun:Requisite.tx: Borrowed from Latin requisita, inflection of requisitus (“required, needed”).

noun:Raubbau.tx: From Raub (“robbing, plunder”) + Bau. The second component is used in the sense of Abbau (“winning, mining”); compare Tagebau.

verb:resignieren.tx: 16th century in the obsolete sense, from Middle French resigner, from Latin resignare. The contemporary since the 18th century, from Modern French résigner.

noun:Rotunde.tx: Borrowed from Latin rotunda, from rotundus. Doublet of Rotunda

noun:Räuberpistole.tx: Räuber + Pistole, in its story sense originally a Berlin colloquialism often in reference to disingenuously constructed crime fiction, also supported by a jargonic verb räubern (“to fib, to tell tall stories”).

verb:riegeln.tx: From Middle High German rigelen (“to bolt, to lock”), from Old High German rigilōn (“to protect”).

verb:röhren.tx: From Middle High German rēren, from Old High German rērēn, from Proto-West Germanic *rairōn (“to roar, cry”). Cognate with Bavarian rearn, Dutch reren, English roar.

noun:Resterampe.tx: Based on the surplus goods chain "Rudis Reste Rampe" (lit. "Rudi's Ramp of Leftovers"), references to which occur starting in the late 1980's in Berlin. The choice of the term Rampe (“ramp”) is likely at least partly motivated by the alliteration, but potentially from the sense of "(un)loading dock", see Laderampe. Early metaphorical applications in the 1990's and early 2000's often still …

noun:Rabatz.tx: Deverbal from rabatzen, now obsolete in favour of Rabatz machen, from Polish rąbać, alternatively or concurrently dialectal rabanzen, rabastern etc. from old ranzen, ratzen going back to Middle High German and ultimately related to onomatopoeic formations such as well-known ratschen and rasseln.

noun:Ramen.tx: Borrowed from Japanese ラーメン (rāmen), from Mandarin 拉麵 /拉面 (lāmiàn).

noun:Rollator.tx: Probably borrowed from English rollator (originally a brand name) at some point in the 1960s. Compare Roller, constructed identically except with the native agent noun suffix instead of one borrowed from Latin.

adj:rabenschwarz.tx: Inherited from Middle High German rabenswarz, by surface analysis, Rabe + schwarz. Literally, “black like a raven”.

phrase:rechts ist, wo der Daumen links i.tx: Literally, “right is where your thumb is on the left”, a nonsensical mnemonic (as it requires the distinction in itself).

noun:Rollmops.tx: From rollen (“to roll”) + Mops (“pugnosed dog”), coined in Berlin.

noun:Reibach.tx: 19th century, via thieves’ cant (Rotwelsch) from Yiddish רוח (reyvakh), from Hebrew רוח (réwaḥ, “profit”).

intj:rubbeldiekatz.tx: From rubbeln + Geldkatze: the act of counting coins by rubbing the outside of one's wallet when making a quick bargain

noun:Reservist.tx: Borrowed from French réserviste; second half of the 19th century. By surface analysis, Reserve + -ist.

phrase:reim dich oder ich fress dich.tx: Literally, “rhyme yourself or I’ll eat you!”, which must be understood as though spoken by the poet to the poem.

verb:rummachen.tx: By surface analysis, rum- (“around”) + machen (“to do, make”).

noun:Rebbe.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish רבי (rebe). Doublet of Rabbi and Rabbiner.

verb:reihern.tx: Reiher (“heron”) + -n, 1860s or 1870s. Compare earlier kotzen wie ein Reiher (“to puke like a heron”), based on herons regurgitating parts of their prey.

verb:reinspucken.tx: From rein- (“in, into, inside”) + spucken (“to spit”). For the idiomatic use, compare synonymous Dutch er niet in spugen.

noun:Rant.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English rant. Cognate to German ranzen (“to romp”).

noun:Rohbau.tx: From roh + Bau. First attested in the 19th century. Equivalent to “raw” + “construction.”

noun:Rentabilität.tx: By surface analysis, rentabel + -ität. Cognate of French rentabilité, Spanish rentabilidad, Portuguese rentabilidade, Catalan rendibilitat, Dutch rendabiliteit, Swedish räntabilitet.

adv:reihum.tx: From Reihe (“sequence”) + um (“in order to, by”).

noun:Rally.tx: Borrowed from English rally, from Middle French rallier.

verb:reinbuttern.tx: From rein- + buttern, literally “to butter in”.

phrase:rum wie num.tx: Literally, "[one way] around as [the other way] around". From the shortened forms of herum and hinum, the latter having fallen out of usage otherwise. Attested in writing by 1891, Küpper broadly dates it to the 19th century. Early attestations are primarily from the East Central German area. Compare also Jacke wie Hose, as well as the not synonymous but similar hüben wie drüben.

noun:Rockstar.tx: Borrowed from English rockstar, equivalent to Rock + Star.
